title: Wazuh 5.0 rc2: eight things that still change for your 4.x custom rules
summary:
Wazuh 5.0.0-rc2 was published on 30 October 2026. If you maintain custom 4.x rules and decoders, the question is whether anything we measured on rc1 moved. We re-ran all eight of those checks on rc2 in a lab with Docker, one manager, one indexer and one 4.14.7 agent. All eight came out the same. GA has not been released, so treat this as a release candidate and not a verdict.

1. The analysis binary has no 4.x rule keywords

We counted occurrences of if_sid, if_matched_sid, same_srcip and frequency in the rc2 wazuh-manager-analysisd binary with grep -a -o piped to wc -l. All four were 0. We also searched the rest of the rc2 bin and lib directories: if_sid, if_matched_sid and same_srcip appear in no file. The 4.14.7 binary contains all of them. We are not quoting its exact counts, because our counting method was not the same across runs.

2. Your XML files load without a word

We dropped 4.x rule, decoder and list XML into both the old etc directories and the new /etc/wazuh-manager, then restarted. The restart produced 116 new log lines (124 on rc1). Zero of them mentioned rules, decoders, lists or xml. wazuh-manager-analysisd -t returned 0 and wazuh-manager-conf validate returned 0. A passing config check does not tell you the rules are doing anything.

3. srcip is rejected as a field

Posting content that uses srcip to the content manager rules endpoint returned HTTP 400: "Error in Security Analytics. The following fields are not part of the Wazuh Common Schema (WCS): [srcip]". Same body, same message as rc1.

4. Unparsed lines are not indexed by default

index_unclassified_events is false in all four spaces (standard, custom, draft, test). We sent 16 log lines: 12 documents were indexed, and the 4 lines from our home-made app, which had no rewritten decoder, were in no index. On rc1 it was also 4 of 16.

5. Indexer flush is 20 seconds

From the binary, the default analysisd.indexer_flush_interval is 20 s, allowed range 1 to 3600. Measured delay from event to visible document was at most 20.2 s, with the sawtooth about 20 s apart. Setting it to 0 is now refused at config load ("Allowed range: 1 to 3600"), and afterwards the manager still listed analysisd as running; on rc1 the same setting stopped analysisd. The "5 s flush gives 7.1 s worst case" figure is from rc1 only. We did not re-run it on rc2.

6. Active response does not reach a 4.14.7 agent

A 4.14.7 agent enrolled and its events were indexed. We then triggered an active response through an indexer monitor. The manager created the task, and remoted logged: "task type 'active_response' not supported for legacy agents, not delivered". The agent's active-responses.log had no active response line. The rc2 release notes add an active response allowlist, which we did not test.

7. Frequency rules have no working replacement yet

Our 4.x frequency rule, rewritten as a Sigma aggregation rule, saved without complaint (HTTP 201). Creating a detector for it returned HTTP 500: "Cannot invoke "java.util.Map.containsKey(Object)" because "this.fieldMappings" is null", a NullPointerException. We tried three times, once after an attempt to add a field mapping, and got the same error each time, so the rule never ran. Two correlation rules also saved (HTTP 201), but after sending our 16 log lines three times and waiting 200 s there were zero correlation alerts. The stock ruleset raised no finding for our nine pre-auth SSH disconnects from one IP. All of this matches rc1. One small difference: the field-mapping request itself now returns HTTP 500, where rc1 returned 200; the detector fails either way.

8. A rewritten child rule fires next to its parent

In 4.x our child rule raised only the child alert for the root-login line. Rewritten in Sigma, with the parent's condition copied into the child, both matched: logtest on that line listed parent-100510 and child-of-100510-user-root, and the detector produced a finding for each on the same event. Same as rc1. In our runs that meant two findings for one event; we have not yet tested excluding the child's case from the parent.

What this does not cover

The "5 s flush gives 7.1 s worst case" figure in item 5 is from rc1 only. Untested on either release candidate: TLS with the security plugin on, multiple nodes, a 5.x agent, CDB lists in the new key-value store, and whether Sigma timeframe is honoured.

One change that will break lab scripts: the rc2 notes say manager configuration moved from /var/wazuh-manager/etc to /etc/wazuh-manager with no symlink, which broke our rc1 lab scripts until we fixed the paths.

What we can run for you and what it costs is on one page: https://vct.atkvn.com/wazuh-5-migration.html

title: Stop Letting AI Code Without Specs: How We Built a 4-Role Autonomous Engineering Framework
summary:
If you've spent any serious amount of time using AI coding assistants like Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, or Windsurf on non-trivial codebases, you've almost certainly experienced these moments of frustration:

  1. Premature Implementation: You describe a broad feature, and the AI immediately starts editing 10 random files without analyzing edge cases or asking for clarification.
  2. Context Window Amnesia: Five prompts into the session, the AI forgets the architectural constraints you established at the start and begins undoing previous logic.
  3. Ghost Fixes & Silent Regressions: The AI claims "I have fixed the issue!", but upon closer inspection, it just broke two other critical components because no independent QA tested it.

We faced these exact challenges while scaling a high-traffic production application to 95–100 Google PageSpeed scores, OWASP Zero-Trust compliance, and strict WCAG accessibility.

To eliminate prompt-drift and hallucinated implementations once and for all, we built and open-sourced Agentic-SDD: A spec-driven multi-agent operating framework that turns single-agent assistants into a disciplined 4-role software engineering team.

🏛️ The 4-Role Operating Lifecycle

Instead of treating the AI as an all-in-one coder that plans, writes, tests, and deploys without oversight, Agentic-SDD strictly separates concerns into 4 independent roles:

┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│   Role 01    │ ──> │   Role 02    │ ──> │   Role 03    │ ──> │   Role 04    │
│   Planner    │     │  Developer   │     │  QA Tester   │     │  Gatekeeper  │
└──────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘
       │                    │                    │                    │
  Clarifies            Implements           Adversarial          Audits diffs
  edge cases           strictly in          boundary tests       & signs off
  & specs plan         Impacted Files       & self-heals         for release

1. 🏛️ Role 01 — System Architect & Planner

  • Rule: Strictly Read-Only on production source code.
  • Workflow: Proactively asks 2–3 edge-case clarification questions (Step 0 Clarifications) before generating a formal technical specification in tracking/plan/_PLAN.md.
  • Output: Scope (In/Out), impacted files table, and testable acceptance criteria.

2. 💻 Role 02 — Software Engineer / Developer

  • Rule: Strictly bound to the Impacted Files declared in the plan (Zero Scope Drift).
  • Workflow: Follows strict web interface guidelines (explicit 60 FPS transitions, zero layout shifts), implements defensive logic with try/catch, and syncs action checklist items (- [x]).

3. 🧪 Role 03 — QA & Quality Engineer

  • Rule: Independent verification; forbidden from touching business logic code directly.
  • Workflow: Executes boundary tests (edge cases, empty inputs, network failure, 4-viewport responsive audits: 430px, 768px, 1024px, 1440px+).
  • Autonomous Self-Healing Loop: If a bug is detected, QA publishes a structured report with root causes. The Orchestrator automatically dispatches Dev to fix and QA to re-test (up to 3 autonomous cycles) until reaching 100% PASS.

4. 🛡️ Role 04 — Strict Tech Lead & Gatekeeper

  • Rule: The only role authorized to approve merges, archive plans, or sign off on releases.
  • Workflow: Audits git diffs against performance regressions, security vulnerabilities, and accessibility standards.

🚀 Why "Markdown-First Persistent State"?

Most multi-agent frameworks force you to set up complex vector databases, Redis queues, or Python orchestration servers.

Agentic-SDD takes the opposite approach: Git & Markdown are all the state you need.

Every handoff is preserved as a permanent artifact in your repo:

  • tracking/plan/: Active technical specifications.
  • tracking/report/: QA audit findings and self-healing logs.
  • tracking/task/: Daily prioritized task board (DAILY_TASKS.md).
  • tracking/log/: Release history (CHANGELOG.md).
  • tracking/done/: Permanent archive of completed specifications.

Result: Zero external dependencies, zero database setup, and zero token waste—agents only read the exact markdown artifact required for their role.

⚡ Try It in 5 Seconds (Zero Dependencies)

We packaged the framework into an ultra-lightweight Node.js CLI (< 50KB, starts in ~100ms) with zero third-party dependencies:

# Initialize into any new or existing project (Next.js, Astro, Vue, Python, Go, etc.)
npx @dzutr/agentic-sdd init --preset fullstack-edge --ide all

# Verify setup integrity across all 5 roles & tracking directories
npx @dzutr/agentic-sdd doctor

# Audit your codebase for UI standards & spec compliance
npx @dzutr/agentic-sdd verify

Universal Multi-IDE Support

One single source of truth (.agent-roles/ and AGENTS.md) generates native bridge adapters for your preferred AI tool:

  • Cursor: .cursor/rules/agentic-sdd.mdc
  • Claude Code: CLAUDE.md
  • Windsurf: .windsurfrules
  • Antigravity: .antigravity/roles/
  • GitHub Copilot: .github/copilot-instructions.md

📦 Open Source & Community

Agentic-SDD is completely free and open-source under the MIT License.

  • 🔗 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/dzutran/agentic-sdd
  • 📦 NPM Package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@dzutr/agentic-sdd

If you find this approach helpful for building disciplined, predictable AI engineering workflows, please consider dropping a Star ⭐ on GitHub to support the project!

We'd love to hear your thoughts: How do you currently prevent AI coding assistants from hallucinating or scope-drifting across long sessions?

title: 16K Neural Image Super-Resolution and Batch E-Commerce Photo Restoration with Monipix
summary:
Upscaling low-resolution product photos, vintage family portraits, or AI-generated concept art using traditional bicubic or Lanczos interpolation inevitably produces blurry edges, halo artifacts, and washed-out textures.

In this technical write-up, we share how we built Monipix — a browser-based AI image upscaler and creative workspace capable of 2x to 16x super-resolution (up to 4K, 8K, and 16K) — along with our HD Image Converter and open-source AI Image Upscaler Toolkit.

1. Tiled Neural Super-Resolution Without GPU OOM

Upscaling a 1024×1024 image by 8x or 16x produces a 16,384×16,384 canvas (268 megapixels). Running a single forward pass at that resolution exhausts VRAM immediately. To achieve artifact-free 16K output:

  1. Overlapping Tile Decomposition: The input image is partitioned into overlapping tiles (e.g., 512×512 with a 64px feathering margin).
  2. Degradation-Aware Restoration: Compression artifacts (JPEG blockiness, mosquito noise, motion blur) are removed prior to high-frequency texture synthesis.
  3. Hann-Window Blending: Upscaled tiles are stitched using raised-cosine weights so tile boundaries are completely invisible even across smooth gradients. 
interface UpscaleOptions {
  scaleFactor: 2 | 4 | 8 | 16;
  targetResolution: "4K" | "8K" | "16K";
  denoiseStrength: number; // 0.0 - 1.0
  faceEnhancement: boolean;
  outputFormat: "png" | "webp" | "jpg";
}

2. High-Frequency Detail Recovery for E-Commerce & Print

For e-commerce catalogs, anime illustrations, and print-ready posters, Monipix and the Monipix HD Image Converter preserve crisp typography, fabric weave, and facial details without over-smoothing.

Developers can also inspect our open-source benchmarks, scripts, and integration examples on GitHub at arkyu2077/ai-image-upscaler.

title: Automating Narrated Whiteboard Explainer Videos from Docs and Scripts with SpeedPainter & MCP
summary:
Creating hand-drawn whiteboard explainer videos from technical documentation, product specs, or classroom notes usually requires hours of manual keyframing in desktop timeline editors.

In this technical guide, we walk through how we built SpeedPainter AI — a browser-based AI speed paint and whiteboard animation studio — and how developers and AI agents can automate narrated multi-scene explainer videos using our AI Whiteboard Explainer Video Maker and open-source SpeedPainter Explainer Video CLI & MCP Server.

1. Stroke-Order Extraction & Hand-Drawn Trajectory Synthesis

Unlike generic text-to-video diffusion models that hallucinate unreadable text or flickering diagrams, a true whiteboard speed-paint animation needs deterministic stroke progression:

  1. Structural Edge & Contour Decomposition: Uploaded diagrams, illustrations, or generated storyboard frames are segmented into hierarchical vector contours (primary outlines first, internal shading and color fills second).
  2. Continuous Path Ordering: We solve a locality-constrained path optimization problem so the virtual drawing hand moves naturally across the canvas without erratic jumps.
  3. Synchronized Voiceover & Subtitle Alignment: In our AI Whiteboard Explainer Video Maker, each script paragraph is synthesized into natural narration while the stroke drawing duration is dynamically scaled to match the audio cadence. 
interface SceneSpec {
  sceneIndex: number;
  narrationText: string;
  visualPrompt: string;
  sketchDurationSec: number;
  handStyle: "marker" | "pencil" | "chalk" | "none";
}

2. Automating Explainer Videos from Claude Desktop & Cursor via MCP

To let developers generate whiteboard animations directly from markdown READMEs or PR descriptions, we open-sourced SpeedPainterOrg/explainer-video.

You can wire it into Claude Desktop, Cursor, or Windsurf via MCP:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "speedpainter": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@speedpainter/explainer-video-mcp"]
    }
  }
}

3. Try It Live

  • Web Studio (Image to Speed Paint Video): https://www.speedpainter.org/en
  • Script-to-Whiteboard Explainer Video Maker: https://www.speedpainter.org/en/explainer-video
  • GitHub Repository & MCP Integration: https://github.com/SpeedPainterOrg/explainer-video

title: VIDRAFT POCKET: Running a 180B MoE Model on an 8 GB VRAM Laptop — 3.15M Downloads and Counting
summary:
VIDRAFT POCKET: Running a 180B MoE Model on an 8 GB VRAM Laptop — 3.15M Downloads and Counting

TL;DR: VIDRAFT POCKET is a family of GGUF-format sparse Mixture-of-Experts models designed to run on consumer hardware — including CPU-only PCs and laptops with as little as 8 GB VRAM — without any modified runtimes or cloud dependency. The flagship POCKET-Darwin-180B achieves 87.65% quality retention at 4-bit quantization, matching its BF16 baseline. With over 3.15 million total Hugging Face downloads, it's worth understanding how it actually works.

What it is

VIDRAFT POCKET is a collection of GGUF-formatted large language models built around three explicit design constraints:

  • Standard-runtime-only: Every file loads into the official, unmodified llama.cpp build — and by extension, Ollama, LM Studio, and PocketPal. No custom forks, no CUDA requirement, no cloud calls.
  • Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture: Only a small fraction of the total network parameters are activated per token, making very large parameter counts (35B, 180B) viable on hardware that would otherwise be completely inadequate.
  • Measured, not estimated, performance: Benchmark numbers are sourced from same-machine, same-binary comparisons rather than theoretical throughput projections.

The family currently includes at least three major repositories on Hugging Face. As of November 1, 2026, those repositories logged a combined 1,113,164 downloads in the prior 30 days and 3,154,913 total downloads. POCKET-Darwin-180B had been live for fewer than 30 days at that point, so its 30-day and lifetime download figures are identical.

How it works

The core engineering insight behind POCKET is that sparse MoE models have a favorable ratio of total parameters to active parameters per forward pass. A 180B-parameter MoE model might activate only a fraction of those weights for any given token, which dramatically reduces the memory bandwidth and compute needed at inference time compared to a dense model of equivalent parameter count.

POCKET packages these models as GGUF files, the standard interchange format for llama.cpp-based runtimes. GGUF supports mixed-precision quantization, allowing different layers or weight groups to be quantized at different bit widths. This is how POCKET-26B achieves near-baseline quality at 2-bit quantization, and how POCKET-Darwin-180B's 4-bit variant matches its BF16 counterpart on quality benchmarks.

One notable operational detail surfaced in the article: when running inference on CPU with llama-cli, the -t flag should be set to physical core count, not logical thread count. Using all hyperthreaded logical cores can significantly decrease throughput rather than increase it — a common footgun when tuning llama.cpp for multi-core CPUs.

Benchmarks & results

All figures below come directly from the source article and reflect same-binary, same-machine comparisons:

Model Hardware Generation speed
POCKET-35B 16-thread Xeon CPU 27.0 tok/s
Comparison model (Bonsai-27B) 16-thread Xeon CPU 10.1 tok/s
POCKET-35B H100 GPU 197 tok/s
Comparison model (Bonsai-27B) H100 GPU 89 tok/s

Note: On H100 prompt processing (prefill), the comparison model was faster — 1,816 tok/s vs. 753 tok/s for POCKET-35B. Generation throughput and prefill throughput are distinct metrics; check both for your use case.

Quantization quality:

  • POCKET-26B at 2-bit with mixed-precision quantization: near-baseline quality score retention
  • POCKET-Darwin-180B at 4-bit: 87.65% on the quality benchmark, matching the BF16 baseline

File sizes and minimum hardware:

  • POCKET-35B Q2_K: 13 GB — runs on a CPU-only PC with standard llama.cpp; measured at 19.5 tok/s on a MacBook M3 Pro CPU
  • POCKET-Darwin-180B 4-bit: 111 GB — measured at 4.17 tok/s on a laptop with 8 GB VRAM + 32 GB RAM; also runnable fully on CPU in a mini-PC with 128 GB RAM

How to try it

POCKET models are publicly available on Hugging Face. Files are standard GGUF and load into any official llama.cpp-based runtime without modification.

Download via Hugging Face CLI:

pip install huggingface_hub
huggingface-cli download  --local-dir ./pocket-model

(Check the official VIDRAFT Hugging Face organization page for exact repository names and recommended quantization variants for your hardware.)

Run with llama.cpp (CPU-only inference):

./llama-cli -m ./pocket-model/.gguf -ngl 0 -t
  • -ngl 0 forces all layers to CPU (no GPU offload)
  • -t should equal your physical core count, not your logical thread count

The same GGUF files are compatible with Ollama, LM Studio, and PocketPal without any extra configuration. For users who prefer not to install anything locally, the article mentions that a POCKET Image Studio option is available for browser-based access within the POCKET collection.

FAQ

Q: Do I need a modified or custom-patched version of llama.cpp?
A: No. The source article explicitly states that the official, unmodified llama.cpp binary loads all POCKET files. This also means compatibility with Ollama, LM Studio, and PocketPal out of the box.

Q: Why does setting -t to logical thread count hurt performance?
A: Hyperthreading shares physical execution resources between logical cores. For memory-bandwidth-bound workloads like LLM inference, saturating physical cores and then adding logical threads creates contention rather than parallelism. Set -t to physical core count for best results.

Q: Is 4.17 tok/s on a 180B model actually usable?
A: That depends on your workload. For interactive chat, 4–5 tok/s is slower than comfortable reading speed but functional. For batch processing or document summarization tasks where you aren't watching tokens stream in real time, it's more practical than it sounds for a 180B model on consumer hardware.

Q: What quality benchmark does the 87.65% figure refer to?
A: The source article does not name the specific benchmark suite. Treat it as an internal quality consistency metric relative to the BF16 baseline, and run your own domain-specific evals before committing to production use.

title: I built a bot that plays my Unreal game and files the bugs
summary:
⭐ GitHub: github.com/grloper/playgoblin · open source (Apache-2.0) · by @grloper

grloper / playgoblin

A goblin plays your game overnight and files the bugs it breaks. Open-source QA bot for Unity, Unreal and any engine, with an MCP server for AI agents.

PlayGoblin

An open-source QA bot that plays your game like a person and files the bugs with evidence.
Unity, Unreal, or any engine that can write a log file. Deterministic checks, no LLM in the loop, no account.


A real 150 s run on a UE 5.8 game (3x time-lapse of seconds 19-52, overlay added). Full run: 251 m walked, 19 waypoints, 12.0% coverage, 1 confirmed and 12 unconfirmed stuck spots.


A frame PlayGoblin captured while walking the town level of a real Unreal Engine 5.8 game (Use Your Friends). Frames and clips like this are attached to findings.

Status: pre-release (0.1.0-dev). Works on Unity 6000.4, and on Unreal 5.8.3 (Win64) with a sample project and one real game Expect rough edges. See Status for exactly what has and has not been verified.

What it catches

These come from real runs, not mock-ups. Most were found by running on a…


View on GitHub


I'm making an indie game in Unreal Engine 5.8, and like most solo developers I have a testing problem: nobody walks the whole game after every change. I do it for ten minutes, see nothing wrong, and ship the build. So I wrote a bot to do the boring part, and I'm releasing it as open source. It is called PlayGoblin, and it is pre-release (0.1.0-dev), so please read the limits section before you get excited.

A real 150 s run on my game, shown as a 3x time-lapse of seconds 19 to 52 (overlay added by me). The full run walked 251 m and reached 19 waypoints, but covered only 12.0% of the 1137 walkable cells; it logged 1 confirmed and 12 unconfirmed stuck spots. Coverage in the overlay is derived from sampled positions. The goblin is not a speedrunner yet.

The problem

Unit tests check what you thought to assert. Recorded input replays only cover the path you recorded and break when the level changes. Manual QA is great, but it does not run at 3 a.m. after every commit. The gap I care about is "nobody walked there": a stuck spot behind a prop, a fall through a missing collision, a menu button wired to nothing, a TODO that made it into a title screen.

What PlayGoblin is

An engine-side component walks the game and writes a plain run folder: events.jsonl plus a summary. A Python CLI reads that folder and produces findings, an HTML report, and optionally GitHub issues. Each finding has evidence, meaning an event, a frame, or a log line. If the bot cannot show it, it does not report it.

There are engine sides for Unity (6000.4 tested) and Unreal (5.8.3 Win64 tested). Any other engine that can write the run-folder format (documented in docs/PROTOCOL.md) gets the same checks and reports. I tested that with a fake Godot-style run, not a real Godot game.

The bugs it found on my game

I ran it on my Unreal game this week. Three results are worth telling honestly.

The player could not move. The game had no input bound to move the pawn. The bot, which reads the game's own key and axis bindings and presses the keys that should move the player, never left the spawn point and reported "The player never moved" as critical.

A bug in the bot, found by the game. My game has a level-sized invisible blocking volume. It hid the ground from every floor probe, so the bot saw nothing walkable. That was a bug in PlayGoblin, not in the game, and the fix is that the bot now skips actors it starts inside and logs them. Real games are weirder than sample projects, and this is why I am asking for run folders from yours.

Grey-box look. It lists visible actors still using /Engine/BasicShapes meshes or the engine grid material and reports each as "Prototype look". It is a cheap way to see how much of a level is still placeholder art.

On the Unreal sample project, which has bugs I planted, it also finds a UMG "Options" button that does nothing and menu text reading "TODO: title". Another false positive taught me something: it flagged a pastel-pink game as missing-material pink. Now only pure magenta counts.

How it works

It plays through real input. In key mode (-PlayGoblinKeys) it presses the game's bound keys, turns with simulated mouse movement rather than setting the camera, taps action keys at irregular intervals, and tries a jump when stuck. If nothing moves the player, or the mouse does nothing after repeated probes, that is itself a finding (dead_input).

It crawls UMG menus. About every two seconds it finds visible widgets, reports placeholder text, and clicks each enabled button once. A button is dead if nothing observable changed within a second.

It explores on purpose. Instead of random destinations it heads for the nearest unvisited ground next to what it has already seen. On the sample project, same seed and 150 seconds, coverage went from 34% to 73% on one level and from 48% to 93% on the other. Every report prints coverage.

The checks have no LLM in them. Each check is a pure function: run folder in, findings out. The same events give the same findings every time, and there are 62 Python tests. A stuck spot only counts as confirmed once it repeats, so one unlucky run does not file a fake bug. An LLM can optionally write a summary paragraph, labelled as such.

Agents can drive it. There is an MCP server (playgoblin mcp) with five tools: status, run, report, findings and file_issues. The repo is also a Claude Code plugin with a skill that teaches an agent when to run it and how to read confidence. Filing GitHub issues is a dry run unless you explicitly confirm.


The HTML report: each finding links to its evidence.

Quickstart 

pip install "git+https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin#subdirectory=cli"   # Python 3.11+

Unreal: copy unreal/PlayGoblin into your project's Plugins/ and launch the game with the flag:

UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe MyGame.uproject -game -playgoblin -PlayGoblinSeconds=300 -PlayGoblinSeed=1 -PlayGoblinOut=D:/runs -PlayGoblinExit
playgoblin report D:/runs/id>     # report.html, report.md, findings.json

Unity: add the package from https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin.git?path=/unity, put the PlayGoblin Player component on your player, press Play, then playgoblin run --minutes 10 --runs 3.

The plugin does nothing unless -playgoblin is on the command line, so shipping with it enabled is harmless.

Honest limits

  • It is pre-release. Unity 6000.4 and Unreal 5.8.3 on Win64 are the only tested combinations.
  • Accuracy on real games is not measured. My samples were written by the people who wrote the checks, so treat them as regression tests. The Unreal plugin passed its sample (all 5 planted bugs, nothing on the clean twin) on one seed and one machine.
  • UMG buttons are clicked by broadcasting OnClicked, so Slate hit testing is not exercised; Enhanced-Input-driven and CommonUI-only menus are not covered.
  • It walks and clicks. It does not judge fun, balance, visuals or audio, and "no findings" never means bug free.

Try it, and help

The most useful contribution right now is running it on a game and telling me what it missed or got wrong, with the run folder attached. Open an issue at https://github.com/grloper/playgoblin. Roadmap items: more real-game runs with published precision numbers, other Unreal versions and Enhanced Input, Unity UI Toolkit and player builds, and a GitHub Action. If you build for another engine, the run-folder format is short; a writer for it is a good first contribution.

title: Decision-Linked Development (DLD) 1.0 Released
summary:
DLD Kit 1.0 (https://github.com/jimutt/dld-kit) is released. Here's a summary of what changed since the 0.x versions, mainly the move to an npm package.

If you missed the original post, DLD (Decision-Linked Development) is a set of skills that make your coding agent record the decisions behind your code, and read them again before it changes anything. It has been about eight months since I started building it, and it's now in use in a number of personal projects and repositories at my day job at Storytel. DLD takes a somewhat relaxed stance, in the sense that it doesn't try to reach for exhaustive specs, and its comment-based @decision annotations, which tie entries from the decision log to code, are its main distinguishing feature from other delta-oriented, spec-driven approaches.

Nowadays (as of November 2026) software factories and attempts to bridge more of the software development lifecycle in an agent-friendly way are on the tip of many people's tongues. DLD does not in its current shape offer much in that area. It has however been injected and used for the code implementation phase of such pipelines, and I'm experimenting in a separate repository with an optional DLD add-on that adds pipeline & orchestration-oriented features to DLD; some of it appears promising, but if integrated into core DLD, they'll likely be oriented more towards solo projects and smaller OSS projects rather than enterprise settings.

From copied skills to an npm package

Before I started releasing DLD as 1.0 release candidates, you'd install DLD by copying a bunch of skills into your repo (or through Tessl), and each skill carried its own bash scripts. It worked and I like the simplicity, but it was a bit clumsy. Bash scripts that need to run on everything from Linux to Windows are not something I want to maintain, and the test suite was turning into something that was not of the most readable kind.

Now DLD is distributed as npm package called dld-kit. In your repo, run:

npx dld-kit init

It asks which agent harnesses your team uses, writes the config, the skills and a short always-on rule, and you commit the result. Teammates don't have to install anything. To upgrade later it's npx dld-kit@latest update. If you'd rather not have the DLD "binary" (not really the correct term for an .mjs file) checked into the repo, you can gitignore it and use npx dld-kit@latest update to bring it in locally.

title: How I Clone My Own Voice on a Laptop With No GPU (Qwen3-TTS)
summary:
Key takeaways

  • A laptop with no GPU can run Qwen3-TTS voice cloning. Expect 3 to 6 seconds of computing per second of speech.
  • Use reference clips of 7 to 15 seconds. About 30 seconds in total was enough for me.
  • If your reference is casual talking, use x-vector only mode, or the clone will copy your hesitations.
  • Generate 3 to 5 takes per line and pick by where the pauses fall.

Tested on: Windows 11 laptop, Intel Core i9-13900H, 32 GB RAM, integrated graphics only (no NVIDIA GPU). Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base, qwen-tts 0.1.1, Python 3.11.

I post short animated videos that explain AI topics, narrated in Chinese. Recording the narration was the slowest part of every video. I stumble, re-record, and takes from different days don't sound the same. I wanted to type the script and get narration in my own voice.

Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, set this up on my laptop. I described what I wanted, listened to the results and made the calls. You can skip the code blocks; the settings that mattered are explained in plain words.

What I used

The model is Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base, an open-source text-to-speech model from Alibaba's Qwen team (Apache-2.0 license, code at github.com/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS). The "Base" version is the one that clones voices. I downloaded the weights from ModelScope, which was by far the fastest source where I live.

It runs through the qwen-tts Python package, version 0.1.1, in a Python 3.11 virtual environment. My system Python was newer than the machine-learning packages supported, so a separate 3.11 environment saved a lot of trouble.

Everything runs on the CPU in float32, with no CUDA and no NVIDIA card.

Step 1: Reference audio from a recording I already had

I didn't record anything new. I had a long screen recording where I was talking, and I cut three clips from it, about 33 seconds in total.

Longer clips sounded more like me. Clips of 7 to 15 seconds gave a clearly closer match than 4-second clips.

If there is music or noise behind your voice, remove it first. On my CPU, the BS-Roformer separation model needed about two hours for three minutes of audio. The Kim_Vocal_2 model in the audio-separator package did the same job in about three minutes.

Step 2: The setting that decides whether it sounds fluent

Qwen3-TTS Base can clone a voice in two ways:

Mode What you give it What it copies
ICL (the default) One clip plus its exact transcript Your voice and the way you spoke in that clip
x-vector only One or more clips, no transcript Only the sound of your voice

I started with ICL because it's the default. The problem was my reference clip: unscripted talking, with hesitations and uneven pace. The clone copied that too. Every line came out with the same stop-start rhythm, and it didn't sound fluent.

Switching to x-vector only mode fixed it. The model keeps my voice but uses its own steadier pacing, which is what narration needs. Since no transcript is needed, I could also feed it several clips at once.

If your reference is clean read-aloud speech, ICL may be fine. If it's casual talking, try x-vector first.

This is a simplified version of the script on my laptop:

import numpy as np, soundfile as sf, torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

torch.set_num_threads(14)  # how many CPU threads to use

model = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained(
    "models/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", device_map="cpu", dtype=torch.float32
)

# Join a few clips of my voice (mono WAV) with a short silence between them
voice, sr = sf.read("my_voice.wav", dtype="float32")
gap = np.zeros(int(0.25 * sr), np.float32)
clips = [(12.0, 23.5), (61.0, 72.7), (130.2, 141.1)]  # start, end in seconds
parts = []
for start, end in clips:
    parts += [voice[int(start * sr):int(end * sr)], gap]
ref = np.concatenate(parts)

# x-vector only: copy the voice, not the rhythm. No transcript needed.
prompt = model.create_voice_clone_prompt(
    ref_audio=(ref, sr), ref_text=None, x_vector_only_mode=True
)

wavs, out_sr = model.generate_voice_clone(
    text=["大家好，今天聊聊怎么用 AI 给视频配音。"],
    language=["Chinese"],
    voice_clone_prompt=prompt,
)
sf.write("line01.wav", wavs[0], out_sr)

For ICL mode you pass one clip, its exact transcript as ref_text, and x_vector_only_mode=False.

Step 3: Make several takes and keep the best one

The same line comes out a little different every time. Some takes pause in the right places, some rush through a comma. So I generate every line 3 to 5 times and pick one.

What I listen for: does it pause at the commas, and does it avoid long gaps in the middle of a phrase. That matters more than small differences in tone.

With twenty-odd lines and several takes each, listening to everything gets tiring. So a script ranks the takes first:

  • It transcribes each take with a speech recognizer (Paraformer, for Chinese) and compares it with the script, to catch swallowed or wrong words.
  • It measures how close the voice is to a separate sample of my real voice that wasn't used for cloning (CAM++ speaker verification).
  • It counts the pauses and compares them with the commas in the line.

Then I only listen to the top few.

How fast is it on a CPU?

From my logs, generating up to six lines per batch: roughly 3 to 6 seconds of computing for each second of speech. One batch produced 37 seconds of speech in 127 seconds; another produced 24 seconds in 147 seconds.

For a two-minute narration that means about 7 to 12 minutes per take, or roughly half an hour for three takes. It's slow, but it runs in the background. Loading the model also takes time, so I generate all the lines in one run.

Smaller things that helped

Some Chinese characters have more than one pronunciation, and the model sometimes picks the wrong one. When that happens I swap in a same-sounding character in the text sent to the model and keep the correct word in the subtitles. For example, 长连接 became 常连接, and 回调 became 回掉.

Not every video needs my voice, either. For quick news videos I use a preset voice from the CustomVoice version of the same model, which needs no reference audio.

Only clone voices you have permission to use

Clone your own voice, or a voice whose owner has agreed. Don't publish a cloned voice of anyone else.

Would a paid service be easier?

Probably. Hosted services such as ElevenLabs need no setup. I have since run the same script through ElevenLabs' free plan, and its stock Mandarin voices sounded more natural than my clone: ElevenLabs free plan vs a local open-source model.

Originally published on Hands-On AI Tools, where I test AI tools on real tasks. Cover: official Qwen3-TTS introduction graphic from the Qwen team's GitHub repository.

title: 评审意见别只写感想：/review 的 5 条硬规则
summary:
说明：本文是整理，不是新实测。内容来自完整版 commands/review.md 原文与 /review 公开 Gist。/review 是 Lite 版 3 条命令之一（Lite 版免费就有 /review、/commit、/test），完整版同款命令，另含其余 7 条命令与三套模板、速查表。本文只讲 /review 这一条，不编造新实测。

1. 先读全再下判断，不确定的意图标 [推测]

/review 的第一步不是给意见，是把涉及的文件读完、理解意图后再说问题。不确定的意图标 [推测]，不按推测扣分。

没读全就评，评出来的多半是“这段代码为什么这样写”而不是“这段代码有什么问题”。接手一段陌生代码时这条尤其重要：先搞清它想干什么，再说它哪里不对。

2. 只说五个维度的真问题，不凑数

五个维度是：正确性（边界、空值、异常路径、并发）、安全（注入、敏感信息、权限、资源未释放）、可读性（命名、函数长度、注释是否说清“为什么”）、性能（只说明显的数量级问题，如 N+1、重复计算、大对象拷贝）、测试（关键分支是否有用例覆盖）。

每个维度只说真问题，某个维度没问题就空着，不为凑齐五个维度硬找。凑出来的意见接手的人改不动，还会把真正的问题淹没。

3. 分级输出，[必须改] 只留 bug 和安全问题

分三级：[必须改]（bug 或安全）/ [建议改]（可读性、性能）/ [可忽略]（个人偏好，最多 2 条）。

风格之争（单引号还是双引号）不在评审里讨论，用 linter 解决；“只想听夸奖”也不要用这个命令，它只说真话。分级的作用是让接手的人先改会出事的，再改可以更好的，最后才看个人偏好。

4. 每条意见固定四段式，给代码片段不只给方向

格式：文件:行号 — 问题一句话 — 为什么这是问题 — 改法建议（给代码片段，不只说“建议优化”）。

示例取自命令自带示例：orders.py:8 — 文件打开后未关闭，异常时泄漏句柄 — 用 with open(...) 包裹：

with open(path) as f:
return json.load(f)

没有“为什么”和“改法”，意见就落不了地；没有文件:行号，意见就找不到位置。评审结论也只有一句话：可合并 / 需修改后合并 / 建议重构。

5. 上限 10 条，超了先重构再评审

超过 10 条说明代码需要重构而不是评审：直接说“建议先重构再评审”并给出重构方向，不要把 30 条意见一次性倒出来。

同样，超过 500 行的大文件不要一次性评审，先拆小、按模块分次评审；代码还没写完、自己都知道是草稿的，先写完再评，半成品评审浪费双方时间。

不用 /review 的场景

  • 代码还没写完、自己都知道是草稿：先写完再评。
  • 只想听夸奖：这个命令只说真话。
  • 超过 500 行的大文件一次性评审：先拆小，按模块分次评审。
  • 风格之争：用 linter 解决，不在评审里讨论。

风格之争（单引号还是双引号）不在评审里讨论，用 linter 解决；“只想听夸奖”也不要用这个命令，它只说真话。分级的作用是让接手的人先改会出事的，再改可以更好的，最后才看个人偏好。

4. 每条意见固定四段式，给代码片段不只给方向

格式：文件:行号 — 问题一句话 — 为什么这是问题 — 改法建议（给代码片段，不只说“建议优化”）。

示例取自命令自带示例：orders.py:8 — 文件打开后未关闭，异常时泄漏句柄 — 用 with open(...) 包裹：

with open(path) as f:
return json.load(f)

没有“为什么”和“改法”，意见就落不了地；没有文件:行号，意见就找不到位置。评审结论也只有一句话：可合并 / 需修改后合并 / 建议重构。

5. 上限 10 条，超了先重构再评审

超过 10 条说明代码需要重构而不是评审：直接说“建议先重构再评审”并给出重构方向，不要把 30 条意见一次性倒出来。

同样，超过 500 行的大文件不要一次性评审，先拆小、按模块分次评审；代码还没写完、自己都知道是草稿的，先写完再评，半成品评审浪费双方时间。

不用 /review 的场景

  • 代码还没写完、自己都知道是草稿：先写完再评。
  • 只想听夸奖：这个命令只说真话。
  • 超过 500 行的大文件一次性评审：先拆小，按模块分次评审。
  • 风格之争：用 linter 解决，不在评审里讨论。

title: I built an AI assistant to understand GitHub codebases
summary:
I built an AI assistant to help developers understand GitHub codebases

When I join an unfamiliar project, I often spend a lot of time searching through files just to understand how things fit together. I wanted to build a tool that could make exploring a codebase easier.

So I built CodeRAG Assistant.

What it does

CodeRAG Assistant lets you:

  • Index a GitHub repository and search its code by meaning or keywords.
  • Ask questions about the codebase in plain English.
  • See relevant source files alongside answers, so you can verify the context.
  • Generate an architecture and onboarding report for a public repository.

What I learned

Building this taught me that answering a question is only part of the experience. It also matters to show where the answer came from, make repository setup straightforward, and handle the small-screen experience carefully.

I’m still improving the product and would love feedback on what feels useful, confusing, or missing.

Try it

  • Live demo: https://coding-assistant-hazel.vercel.app/

I’m the creator of CodeRAG Assistant. If you try it, please let me know what you think!
